To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Salinian block is underlain by a 26 km thick crust; 2) the crustal structure is similar to that of the Sierra Nevada batholith; 3) a strong seismic anisotropic layer is present in the lower crust; 4) the seismic fabric is inconsistent with recent motion on the San Andreas fault and is likely to be a remnant fabric from past eastward subduction; and 5) the seismic anisotropics fabric is

(a) the crust is 26 km thick with a low velocity (1.88), high VP/VS layer (1.75) at the base of the crust, (b) the lower crust is highly anisotropic, and (c) the anisotropic fabric has an ENE dip, which is inconsistent with recent San Andreas fault slip sense.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and anisotropy of the lower crust in the vicinity of Parkfield, CA.
the crustal structure and seismic properties near the San Andreas fault in central California.
the crustal structure of the Salinian Block in the vicinity of the San Andreas fault near Parkfield.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence that the San Andreas fault zone has a low-velocity zone in its upper crust, but there is evidence that it has a low- velocity zone in the mid-crust.

the crustal thickness and velocity structure of the Salinian block at Parkfield is consistent with that of the surrounding region and the crustal structure of the San Andreas fault zone at Parkfield is characterized by a low velocity, highly anisotropic lower crust.

the crustal structure and seismic velocity anisotropy in the region of the San Andreas fault at Parkfield is complex, with multiple layers that may be associated with the tectonically active San Andreas fault zone, the older Salinian terranes to the west, and the older Franciscan terranes to the east.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the crustal thickness is ∼26 km, the middle crustal velocity increases with depth, the lower crust is highly anisotropic and the anisotropic fabric dips to the ENE.
the crustal structure and seismic properties of the Parkfield area are consistent with the hypothesis that the SAF is a major, but not the only, tectonic boundary in the region.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the San Andreas Fault is not the primary cause of the lower crustal seismic anisotrophy.
RF data are a powerful means of detecting and characterizing seismic anisotropies.
the crustal structure and lower crustal anistropy near Parkfield is consistent with the hypothesis that the San Andreas Fault is located on the eastern boundary of the Farallon slab.
